slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The fail-safe/fail-open distinction traces to Saltzer & Schroeder's 1975 paper 'The Protection of Information in Computer Systems,' which articulated fail-safe defaults as a core security design principle. Misconception: Students assume 'network attack' means an attacker somewhere far away on the internet. Many of these attacks (sniffing, ARP spoofing) require a local foothold, physical access, a rogue Wi-Fi client, or a compromised device on the same segment.

content_blocks: Network-level exploits do not trick a person into clicking a link. They exploit design assumptions baked into protocols standardized decades ago, when the internet's user base was a small and mutually trusting group of researchers. The foundational insight of this topic is that core networking protocols were engineered for functional correctness and resilience against random failure, not against an actively malicious participant sharing the same physical medium.

Security engineers formalize this as the difference between fail-safe and fail-open design. A fail-safe system defaults to a secure state when something breaks; a fail-open system defaults to an available state. Most legacy protocols are fail-open because early internet engineering prioritized availability over confidentiality. ARP is the textbook example: any device on a segment can claim ownership of any IP address, and its neighbors believe it without verification.
The topic is organized around five exploit families: packet sniffing, ARP spoofing, man-in-the-middle interception, denial-of-service, and network-borne malware propagation.

slides.title: The OSI Model as a Map of Attack Surface
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Most network exploits in this course sit at Layer 2 (ARP), Layer 3 (IP), or Layer 4 (TCP/UDP). The application-layer attacks appear in later units.

Misconception: Students memorize the seven layers as trivia. The payoff is diagnostic: knowing the layer tells you the containment boundary and the control family.

Analogy: Think of the layers like the postal system, the envelope's local sorting facility (Layer 2) versus the national routing network (Layer 3). A prank confined to your local post office cannot reach another city.

Exam tip: Memorize a mnemonic (e.g., 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away') but be ready to place a named protocol at its layer and reason about containment.
bullets: Seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application (ISO/IEC 7498-1)
Layer determines blast radius: A Layer 2 attack is confined to one broadcast domain; a Layer 3+ attack can traverse the routed internet
Layer 2 (Data Link): ARP, MAC addresses, Ethernet frames, local segment only
Layer 3 (Network): IP addressing and routing, global reach
Layer 4 (Transport): TCP/UDP, connection state, ports, the SYN flood target
Defense follows layer: The layer of an attack dictates which controls can stop it

content_blocks: Understanding network-level exploits requires fluency in the OSI reference model, because the layer at which an attack occurs determines both its blast radius and its available defenses. The OSI model is a conceptual seven-layer framework used to describe how data moves through a network stack, it is a teaching abstraction, not a protocol. Real stacks like TCP/IP compress several OSI layers together.

An attack executed at Layer 2, the local Ethernet segment, is inherently confined to that broadcast domain. ARP spoofing cannot be launched from across the internet. By contrast, a reflection-based denial-of-service attack executed at Layer 3/4 can be launched from anywhere and target any reachable IP on Earth.
This layered thinking is the conceptual backbone of the entire unit. When you diagnose or defend against an exploit, your first question should always be: at what layer does this operate?

slides.title: Active vs. Passive Attacks
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The active/passive taxonomy is standard in security curricula and maps cleanly onto the CIA triad, passive attacks threaten confidentiality; active attacks threaten integrity and availability.

Misconception: Students think 'undetectable' means 'unstoppable.' Passive sniffing is hard to detect but easy to defeat: end-to-end encryption makes captured traffic useless.

Analogy: Passive is a wiretap that only listens; active is someone splicing the line to inject their own voice. The listener is silent; the splicer creates clicks and pops.

Exam tip: When asked to defend against sniffing, lead with encryption (defeats passive capture) rather than detection, detection barely helps against a purely passive adversary.
bullets: Passive attack: Observation only, the attacker captures traffic without altering it (e.g., simple sniffing)
Detectability: Passive attacks leave no modified traffic behind, making them extremely hard to detect
Active attack: The attacker injects, modifies, or replays traffic, changing network or session state
Footprint: Active attacks leave traces, unexpected ARP replies, malformed packets, unusual retransmissions
Examples: ARP poisoning, SYN floods, and worm propagation are all active; passive sniffing on a shared medium is not
Detection implication: IDS sensors are tuned to catch the footprint of active attacks

content_blocks: Within the network context, a crucial classification separates active attacks from passive attacks. A passive attack involves no interaction with the victim, the adversary merely observes traffic, for example by sniffing a shared medium. Because nothing is modified or injected, passive attacks are correspondingly difficult to detect; there is no anomalous traffic to alert on, only anomalous physical or logical access.

An active attack, by contrast, requires the attacker to inject forged or malformed traffic into the network. ARP cache poisoning, a SYN flood, or a self-replicating worm all leave a detectable, if often subtle, footprint. This footprint is exactly what intrusion detection systems are tuned to recognize.

This distinction matters for defense strategy: passive threats are addressed primarily through encryption and physical/logical access control, while active threats are addressed through detection, validation, and rate limiting.

slides.title: Packet Sniffing and Promiscuous Mode
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Wireshark was originally released as 'Ethereal' in 1998, renamed in 2006. libpcap (WinPcap/Npcap on Windows) is the underlying capture engine shared by nearly every packet tool.

Misconception: Students believe enabling promiscuous mode magically reveals all network traffic. It only reveals frames that reach the card, on a switched network that is mostly your own traffic plus broadcasts.

Analogy: Promiscuous mode is like removing the filter that makes you ignore conversations not addressed to you. But if you are in a soundproof booth (a switch port), removing the filter changes nothing, you still hear only what is piped to you.

Exam tip: A favorite trap: 'A student enables promiscuous mode on a switched LAN but sees only broadcast traffic, why?' The answer is switch forwarding by CAM table, not a broken sniffer.

Promiscuous mode: Disables that filter, the NIC passes every frame it physically receives up to the OS
Monitor mode: The wireless equivalent, additionally exposing 802.11 management/control frames
Capture tools: Wireshark (GUI) and tcpdump (CLI) both build on the libpcap capture library

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Wireshark was originally released as 'Ethereal' in 1998, renamed in 2006. libpcap (WinPcap/Npcap on Windows) is the underlying capture engine shared by nearly every packet tool.

content_blocks: A network interface card normally discards any Ethernet frame not addressed to its own MAC address, filtering unwanted traffic in hardware before the operating system ever sees it. Placing the NIC into promiscuous mode disables that filter, allowing a sniffing application such as Wireshark or tcpdump to capture and display every frame that physically reaches the interface.

On Linux this is enabled with ip link set eth0 promisc on. On wireless adapters the analogous capability is called monitor mode, which additionally exposes the 802.11 management and control frames that carry beacons, association requests, and deauthentication frames.

Crucially, promiscuous mode only yields useful traffic if the frames actually arrive at the interface. Whether they do depends entirely on the physical topology of the network, a hub delivers everything, while a switch delivers almost nothing beyond your own traffic.

slides.title: Hubs vs. Switches: Why Topology Decides What You Can Sniff

quiz.question: An attacker connects a laptop in promiscuous mode to an unused port on a modern enterprise switch and is disappointed to capture only ARP broadcasts and their own web traffic. Which mechanism best explains this outcome?
options: The switch encrypts all unicast frames end-to-end before forwarding them
The switch forwards unicast frames only out the port mapped to the destination MAC in its CAM table
Promiscuous mode is silently disabled by managed switches on connection
The attacker's NIC cannot decode frames from other manufacturers
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct. A switch consults its CAM table and forwards each unicast frame only to the port where the destination MAC was learned, so the attacker never physically receives traffic between other hosts, only broadcasts, multicasts, and their own traffic reach the port. Option A is wrong: switches do not encrypt frames. Option C is wrong: promiscuous mode is a NIC/OS setting the switch cannot disable. Option D is wrong: frames are decoded independent of manufacturer.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SPAN = Switched Port Analyzer (local); RSPAN/ERSPAN extend mirroring across switches. NIDS tools like Zeek and Suricata typically obtain traffic via a SPAN port or a network TAP.

Misconception: That switches were designed as a security control. Switching is a performance optimization; the confidentiality benefit is incidental, and defeatable via ARP spoofing or CAM overflow.

Analogy: A hub is a room where every conversation is broadcast over loudspeakers. A switch is a building of private phone lines, but the operator's switchboard (CAM table) can be tricked or overwhelmed.

Exam tip: Know the CAM table's role. The next slide's MAC flooding attack targets exactly this table.
bullets: Hub (Layer 1): Obsolete device that electrically repeats every incoming signal to all ports, one giant collision domain
On a hub: An attacker on any port receives a copy of all traffic 'for free'
Switch (Layer 2): Learns which MAC lives on which port and forwards unicast frames only to the destination port
CAM table: The switch's lookup table mapping learned MAC addresses to physical ports, populated by observing source MACs
On a switch: A plain sniffer sees only broadcast, multicast, and its own unicast traffic, a real security improvement
Legitimate capture: Admins use port mirroring / SPAN to copy traffic to a monitoring port

content_blocks: Whether promiscuous mode yields useful traffic depends entirely on physical topology. On a legacy hub-based network, every frame is physically replicated to every port, so an attacker plugged into any port receives all traffic on the segment. Hubs turn an entire segment into one collision domain and have been almost entirely replaced by switches since the early 2000s, for both performance and security reasons.

Modern switches forward unicast frames only to the specific port associated with the destination MAC in the switch's CAM (Content Addressable Memory) table. The switch learns these mappings dynamically by inspecting the source MAC of every incoming frame. Consequently, a plain sniffer on a switched network sees only broadcast traffic, multicast traffic, and unicast traffic addressed to its own port.

To legitimately capture traffic across a switched segment, administrators configure port mirroring, SPAN in Cisco terminology, which copies traffic from source ports to a destination port where an IDS sensor or capture appliance is attached. An attacker without admin access to the switch cannot do this and must resort to Layer 2 manipulation instead.

slides.title: MAC Flooding: Turning a Switch Back Into a Hub
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The classic tool is macof (part of dsniff), which can generate hundreds of thousands of forged MACs per minute. Port security is the direct Layer 2 countermeasure.

Misconception: That switches make sniffing impossible. MAC flooding shows the protection is soft, it depends on a finite table with fail-open behavior.

Analogy: Imagine a receptionist with a limited notepad of who-sits-where. Flood them with thousands of fake names until the pad is full; overwhelmed, they resort to shouting every message down every hallway.

Exam tip: Link MAC flooding to the fail-open theme from the opening slides. The exam rewards connecting a specific attack back to the underlying design principle.
bullets: CAM table is finite: Commonly a few thousand to tens of thousands of entries
The attack: Flood the switch with frames bearing thousands of forged, random source MAC addresses
Table exhaustion: Once the CAM table is full, the switch cannot learn or store legitimate mappings
Fail-open fallback: For unknown destination MACs, the switch floods frames to all ports, like a hub
Result: The attacker's sniffer now receives unicast traffic it was never meant to see
Defense: Port security limits the number of MACs per port and shuts the port on violation

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The classic tool is macof (part of dsniff), which can generate hundreds of thousands of forged MACs per minute. Port security is the direct Layer 2 countermeasure.

Misconception: That switches make sniffing impossible. MAC flooding shows the protection is soft, it depends on a finite table with fail-open behavior.

content_blocks: Why can an attacker defeat a switch's incidental confidentiality benefit without any admin access? Because the CAM table is a finite resource, and the switch's behavior when that resource is exhausted is fail-open, not fail-safe.

In a CAM table overflow attack, MAC flooding, the attacker deliberately transmits a high rate of frames, each carrying a different forged random source MAC address. The switch dutifully tries to learn each one, and the table fills. Once full, the switch can no longer store the mapping for legitimate destinations. When a frame arrives for a destination whose port it cannot look up, the switch falls back to flooding the frame out every port, exactly like a hub. The attacker's sniffer now receives traffic destined for other hosts.

This is a perfect illustration of a fail-safe assumption becoming fail-open under resource exhaustion. The standard defense is port security, which limits the number of MAC addresses allowed on an access port and takes a configured action (shutdown, restrict, or protect) when the limit is exceeded.

slides.title: How ARP Works: Broadcast Request, Unicast Reply
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: ARP operates at the Layer 2/3 boundary and is confined to a single broadcast domain. This confinement is central to why segmentation limits ARP attacks.

Misconception: Students think ARP requests are routed. They are not, broadcasts do not cross routers, so ARP is inherently local.

Analogy: ARP is shouting in an apartment building, 'Who lives in unit 20?' and trusting whoever shouts back, with no way to check their ID.

Exam tip: Emphasize 'stateless and unauthenticated', those two words are the root cause of every ARP attack and are exactly what earns credit on an explanation question.
bullets: Purpose: ARP resolves a known IPv4 address into the MAC address needed to deliver an Ethernet frame locally (RFC 826, 1982)
Request: Host A broadcasts 'Who has 192.168.1.20? Tell 192.168.1.10' to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
Reply: Host B recognizes its own IP and unicasts back its MAC address
Caching: Both hosts store the IP-to-MAC mapping in a local ARP cache to avoid repeating the exchange
View it: ip neigh show (Linux) or arp -a (Windows)
IPv6 note: IPv6 replaces ARP with NDP (RFC 4861), which has analogous spoofing risks

slides.title: How ARP Works: Broadcast Request, Unicast Reply
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: ARP operates at the Layer 2/3 boundary and is confined to a single broadcast domain. This confinement is central to why segmentation limits ARP attacks.

Misconception: Students think ARP requests are routed. They are not, broadcasts do not cross routers, so ARP is inherently local.

content_blocks: The Address Resolution Protocol, standardized in RFC 826 in 1982, bridges Layer 3 addressing and Layer 2 delivery. When Host A needs to send an IP packet to Host B on the same subnet but knows only B's IP address, A broadcasts an ARP Request, 'Who has 192.168.1.20? Tell 192.168.1.10', to the Ethernet broadcast address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF. Host B, recognizing its own IP in the request, unicasts an ARP Reply containing its MAC address back to A.

Both hosts then cache the resulting IP-to-MAC mapping locally, so they need not repeat the broadcast for every subsequent packet. Cache entries typically expire after a short timeout ranging from 60 to 1200 seconds depending on the operating system.

ARP predates virtually every modern security consideration. It contains no authentication, no sequence numbers, and no integrity protection of any kind, a design that made perfect sense in 1982 and is catastrophic on an untrusted segment today.

slides.title: Why ARP Is Exploitable: Stateless, Unauthenticated, Gratuitous
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Gratuitous ARP is described informally around RFC 5227 (IPv4 Address Conflict Detection), though the convention predates it. Legitimate failover and malicious poisoning use the identical packet.

Misconception: Students think a poisoned host was somehow 'tricked into asking.' No request is needed at all, that is the whole point of gratuitous ARP abuse.

Analogy: Imagine mailboxes where anyone can walk up and relabel whose name goes with which slot, and everyone just believes the newest label.

Exam tip: If asked why a defense like Dynamic ARP Inspection is needed, root the answer in 'stateless + unauthenticated + gratuitous ARP.' Those three properties are the exam's key terms.
bullets: Stateless: A host accepts and caches an ARP reply even if it never sent a corresponding request
Unauthenticated: No cryptographic way to verify the reply came from the true MAC owner
Gratuitous ARP: A host may announce an IP-to-MAC mapping unprompted, legitimately used for failover and conflict detection
The abuse: Gratuitous ARP lets an attacker unilaterally overwrite every host's cache on the segment
Contrast with TCP: TCP uses sequence/ack numbers precisely to reject unsolicited or out-of-order segments

content_blocks: The critical vulnerability is that ARP is entirely stateless and unauthenticated. A host will accept and cache an ARP reply even if it never issued the corresponding request, and it has no cryptographic means to verify that the reply actually came from the legitimate MAC owner of that IP.

This is compounded by gratuitous ARP, a legitimate feature that lets a host announce or update its own IP-to-MAC mapping without being asked. Gratuitous ARP has valid uses: announcing a new IP, detecting IP conflicts, or updating peers after a failover event in protocols like VRRP and HSRP. But because ARP has no authentication, this same mechanism is trivially abused to unilaterally overwrite the cache of every host on the segment.

The contrast with TCP is instructive. TCP uses sequence and acknowledgment numbers specifically so a receiver can reject segments it did not expect. ARP has no such mechanism, every reply is taken at face value.

slides.title: ARP Cache Poisoning: The Four-Stage Attack Chain
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Tools like arpspoof (dsniff), Ettercap, and Bettercap automate this. NIST and MITRE increasingly use 'adversary-in-the-middle' / 'on-path attacker' rather than the older gendered term.

Misconception: That poisoning breaks connectivity. Done correctly with IP forwarding it is invisible, the victim browses normally while being intercepted.

Analogy: A dishonest mail carrier convinces both you and the post office that they are the correct handoff point, reads all your mail, then delivers it onward so you never notice.

Exam tip: The four-stage sequence is a common free-response prompt. Memorize it as: poison victim → poison gateway → both caches wrong → enable forwarding. Then name the countermeasure (DAI).
bullets: Stage 1: Attacker sends forged ARP replies to the victim claiming the attacker's MAC owns the gateway's IP
Stage 2: Attacker sends forged ARP replies to the gateway claiming the attacker's MAC owns the victim's IP
Stage 3: Both caches update; all victim↔gateway traffic now physically transits the attacker
Stage 4: Attacker enables IP forwarding to relay traffic onward transparently, connectivity is preserved
Result: An on-path (man-in-the-middle) position enabling silent capture or active tampering
MITRE mapping: T1557.002, Adversary-in-the-Middle: ARP Cache Poisoning

content_blocks: An ARP spoofing attack chain proceeds in four stages. First, the attacker, who must already be present on the local segment, sends forged gratuitous ARP replies to the victim, claiming that the attacker's MAC address owns the default gateway's IP. Second, the attacker simultaneously sends forged replies to the gateway, claiming to own the victim's IP. Third, both the victim and gateway update their ARP caches with the false mappings, so all traffic between them now physically transits the attacker's machine.

Fourth, and this is what makes the attack stealthy, the attacker enables IP forwarding on their own machine, relaying traffic onward transparently. Connectivity is preserved, so nothing appears broken to the victim, while every packet is silently duplicated for inspection or modification. This is the canonical way to establish an on-path (man-in-the-middle) position on a local network.

slides.title: Man-in-the-Middle and SSL Stripping
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SSL stripping is why 'the padlock' is a weak signal for users, its absence is easy to miss. HSTS preload closes the first-request gap that sslstrip depends on.

Misconception: That HTTPS alone defeats an on-path attacker. It does, but only if the browser actually negotiates TLS. SSL stripping prevents that negotiation from ever starting.

Analogy: A translator who is supposed to relay your sealed letters instead opens them, reads them, reseals a copy for the recipient, and hands you back an unsealed version so you never realize the seal was broken.

bullets: On-path position: Achieved via ARP poisoning or a rogue access point, enables passive logging or active tampering

content_blocks: Once an attacker holds an on-path position, via ARP poisoning or a rogue access point (Topic 3.2), they can passively log traffic or actively tamper with it. A particularly potent active technique is SSL stripping, a downgrade attack that exploits how users actually browse.

Most users type a bare domain like bank.com without specifying https://. The browser therefore issues its first request over insecure HTTP before any redirect to HTTPS occurs. The on-path attacker intercepts this first plaintext request and thereafter proxies the session: it keeps the victim on HTTP while transparently maintaining a proper encrypted HTTPS session with the legitimate server. It rewrites HTTPS links in the served page down to HTTP so the victim's browser never negotiates its own TLS. The victim sees a working page, often with no padlock, while the attacker reads and can modify everything.

The modern defense is HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), which instructs browsers to only ever contact a site over HTTPS. Preload lists bake this rule into the browser so even the very first request is secure.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: DHCP snooping and DAI are Cisco Catalyst features with equivalents from other vendors. The dependency order matters: DAI without DHCP snooping has no trusted table to check against (unless static ARP ACLs are configured).

Misconception: That DAI inspects data traffic. It inspects only ARP packets, the control-plane messages that populate caches.

Analogy: DHCP snooping is the front desk recording who was officially assigned each apartment; DAI is the guard who checks every 'I live in unit 20' claim against that official ledger before letting it stand.

Exam tip: State the dependency explicitly: DAI relies on the DHCP-snooping binding table. Examiners award credit for naming both together.

Binding table: Maps legitimate IP ↔ MAC ↔ port from the DHCP handshake
Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI): Validates every ARP packet on untrusted ports against that binding table
Enforcement: ARP packets whose claimed mapping does not match a known lease are dropped and logged
Configuration: Per-VLAN, e.g. ip arp inspection vlan 10, DAI depends on DHCP snooping being enabled first
Complements: Port security and VLAN segmentation shrink the blast radius further

content_blocks: The primary standardized defense against ARP spoofing is Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), which removes the trust-by-default assumption at the switch. Rather than forwarding every ARP packet unconditionally, DAI intercepts ARP packets on untrusted ports and validates the claimed IP-to-MAC binding against a trusted binding table before forwarding. Any ARP packet whose mapping does not match a known legitimate binding is dropped and logged.

DAI's binding table does not appear by magic, it is built by DHCP snooping. DHCP snooping designates ports facing legitimate DHCP servers as trusted and end-host ports as untrusted, then observes the DHCP handshake to record which IP was legitimately leased to which MAC on which port. DAI consults this table to decide whether an ARP claim is truthful.

Both features are configured per-VLAN on managed enterprise switches and align with NIST SP 800-53 SC-7 boundary protection guidance. In combination with port security and VLAN segmentation, they form a robust Layer 2 defense.

slides.title: Denial of Service: Targeting Availability
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The three-layer DoS taxonomy (volumetric / protocol / application) is standard and maps to distinct mitigations. Distributed DoS (DDoS) simply means the traffic originates from many sources, typically a botnet.

Misconception: Students equate DoS with 'sending a lot of data.' Application-layer attacks can be low-bandwidth yet devastating because each request is expensive to serve.

Analogy: Volumetric = clogging every lane of the highway; protocol = filling every parking spot with abandoned cars; application-layer = sending customers who each demand a two-hour custom order.

Volumetric: Saturate bandwidth with junk traffic, measured in Gbps/Tbps
Protocol: Exhaust finite state tables in network stacks (e.g., SYN flood), measured in packets/second

content_blocks: Whereas sniffing and man-in-the-middle attacks target confidentiality, denial-of-service (DoS) attacks target availability. The goal is to make a system or network resource unavailable to legitimate users, typically by exhausting a finite resource, CPU, memory, connection-table slots, or bandwidth, rather than by breaching confidentiality or integrity.

DoS attacks are conventionally classified into three layers. Volumetric attacks simply saturate available bandwidth with high-throughput junk traffic, measured in gigabits or terabits per second. Protocol attacks, such as SYN floods, exhaust finite state tables in network stacks rather than raw bandwidth, and are measured in packets per second. Application-layer attacks, such as HTTP floods that repeatedly request computationally expensive dynamic pages, exhaust web server or database resources with comparatively low traffic volume, measured in requests per second.
Recognizing which resource is under attack is the key to choosing the right mitigation, bandwidth scrubbing, SYN cookies, or application rate limiting respectively.

slides.title: The SYN Flood and the TCP Three-Way Handshake

quiz.question: A web server under attack shows a rapidly filling SYN backlog queue and refuses new connections, yet its inbound bandwidth utilization remains modest. Which mitigation most directly addresses this specific attack?
options: Contracting a high-capacity DDoS scrubbing service to absorb bandwidth
Enabling SYN cookies so connection state is not allocated until the handshake completes
Deploying HSTS to force clients onto HTTPS
Enabling Dynamic ARP Inspection on the access switches
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct. The symptom, a filling backlog queue with modest bandwidth, is a protocol-layer SYN flood exhausting connection-state memory. SYN cookies defer state allocation until the final ACK proves the handshake completed, defeating spoofed half-open floods. Option A addresses volumetric (bandwidth) attacks, which this is not. Option C addresses TLS downgrade, unrelated to connection exhaustion. Option D is a Layer 2 anti-spoofing control, irrelevant to TCP backlog exhaustion.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The 1996 Panix ISP attack first widely publicized SYN floods. SYN cookies (RFC 4987) are enabled by default in modern Linux via net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies.

Misconception: That a SYN flood works by sheer bandwidth. It works by exhausting a small, finite table, a low-bandwidth flood of packets can suffice.

Analogy: Calling a receptionist repeatedly, saying 'please hold' each time, and hanging up, every call ties up a line until no real caller can get through. SYN cookies are like taking no notes until the caller proves they are real.

Exam tip: Contrast the resource exhausted (connection-state memory) with a volumetric attack's target (bandwidth). Examiners specifically test this distinction.
bullets: Handshake: Client SYN → server SYN-ACK (allocates state) → client ACK (connection established), RFC 9293
The attack: Flood SYNs, often with spoofed source IPs, and never send the completing ACK
Half-open connections: Each SYN forces the kernel to allocate a control block in the finite backlog/SYN queue
Exhaustion: Once the backlog fills, the server drops new SYNs, legitimate clients cannot connect
Resource consumed: Kernel connection-state memory, not bandwidth
Mitigation: SYN cookies (RFC 4987) defer state allocation until the handshake is provably complete

content_blocks: The classic protocol-layer DoS is the SYN flood, which abuses the mechanics of the TCP three-way handshake defined in RFC 9293. Normally the client sends a SYN, the server replies with a SYN-ACK while allocating state for the half-open connection, and the client completes the exchange with a final ACK.

In a SYN flood, the attacker, often spoofing the source IP so replies never return and never trigger a completing ACK or reset, sends a high rate of SYN packets. Each SYN causes the victim's kernel to allocate a control block in its finite connection backlog (SYN) queue and reply with a SYN-ACK, waiting for an ACK that never arrives. Once the backlog fills, the server can no longer accept legitimate connections.

The resource exhausted is kernel connection-state memory, not bandwidth, which is why a SYN flood is measured in packets per second. The standard mitigation is SYN cookies: instead of allocating memory on the initial SYN, the server cryptographically encodes connection state into the SYN-ACK's sequence number and only allocates real state once the client's ACK proves the handshake completed.

slides.title: Reflection and Amplification Attacks
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: BCP 38 is deceptively simple and enormously effective, if universally deployed, it would eliminate spoofed-source reflection attacks. Incomplete adoption is why these attacks persist.

Misconception: That the reflecting servers are compromised. They are not, they are behaving normally; the attacker merely lies about the source address.

Analogy: Mailing hundreds of postcards to businesses that each reply with a heavy catalog, but writing the victim's return address on every card so all the catalogs land in the victim's mailbox.

Exam tip: Tie amplification to UDP's spoofability and to BCP 38 as the root-cause fix. Contrast with TCP, whose handshake prevents this.
bullets: Reflection: Attacker spoofs the victim's IP as source; a third-party server sends its reply to the victim
Amplification: The reply is far larger than the request, multiplying the attacker's effective bandwidth
Why UDP: Connectionless UDP services permit trivial source-IP spoofing (no handshake to complete)
DNS amplification: Small ANY/DNSSEC query yields ~28–54x larger response
NTP amplification: The legacy monlist command has achieved factors exceeding 500x
Mitigation: Source address validation (BCP 38 / RFC 2827) at the edge; disable open resolvers (BCP 140)

content_blocks: Large-scale volumetric attacks are frequently launched by botnets and further magnified through reflection and amplification. In a reflection attack, the attacker sends a request to a third-party server with the victim's IP spoofed as the source; the server, believing the victim asked, sends its reply directly to the victim. 'Reflection' describes the redirected response. 'Amplification' describes the fact that the response is disproportionately larger than the request, multiplying the attacker's effective bandwidth.

These attacks exploit connectionless UDP-based services because UDP has no handshake and therefore permits trivial source-IP spoofing. DNS amplification abuses open recursive resolvers: a small query for a record type with a large response (ANY or DNSSEC) yields roughly 28–54x amplification. NTP amplification via the legacy monlist command has historically exceeded 500x.

The best mitigations sit at the network edge. Source address validation (BCP 38 / RFC 2827) prevents spoofed-source packets from ever leaving a network, and disabling open recursive resolvers (BCP 140) removes the reflectors themselves.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Mirai's source code was released publicly in September 2016 by 'Anna-senpai,' spawning countless derivative botnets. It compromised an estimated 600,000+ devices at peak.

content_blocks: On October 21, 2016, Dyn, a major managed DNS provider, was hit with a sustained DDoS that rendered Twitter, Netflix, Reddit, Spotify, GitHub, and others unreachable for large portions of the U.S. East Coast for most of a business day. Because these companies had outsourced authoritative DNS resolution to Dyn, taking down Dyn functionally took the sites offline, even though the sites' own servers were perfectly healthy.

The attack was generated by the Mirai botnet, which had compromised hundreds of thousands of poorly secured IoT devices by scanning the internet for open Telnet ports and trying a small hardcoded list of default factory credentials. Each compromised device joined a command-and-control network that directed synchronized floods estimated to exceed 1 Tbps.

The incident is academically significant for two reasons. First, it exposed a supply-chain fragility: a single third-party dependency became a single point of failure cascading across unrelated companies. Second, it showed that the weakest link is often consumer IoT with no security lifecycle, no patching, no forced credential rotation, and little manufacturer incentive to harden.

slides.title: Network Worms and Lateral Movement
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SMBv1, the oldest and most vulnerable dialect, was disabled by default starting with Windows 10 version 1709 (2017) in direct response to EternalBlue-based worms.

Misconception: Students blur worms and viruses. The defining line is user interaction: worms need none; viruses generally do.

Analogy: A virus is a cold that spreads only when someone shakes an infected hand (user action). A worm is airborne, it spreads on its own to anyone in the room (any reachable vulnerable host).

Exam tip: When classifying malware, cite the mechanism (autonomous exploitation of a network service) rather than the symptom. That is how examiners separate worms from viruses and from DoS.
bullets: Worm: Self-replicating malware that spreads autonomously with no user interaction
Mechanism: Scan for a remotely reachable vulnerable service, exploit it, copy itself, repeat
Virus contrast: A virus needs a host file and usually user action (opening an attachment) to spread
Lateral movement: Moving from an initial foothold to other internal systems (MITRE TA0008)
Common vector: Server Message Block (SMB) over TCP 445, a frequent RCE target in Windows environments
Worms vs. humans: Worms automate lateral movement; ransomware crews often do it manually

slides.speaker_notes:

content_blocks: Distinct from denial of service, network worms exploit vulnerable network-facing services to spread copies of themselves from host to host with no user interaction. The process, scan for a reachable vulnerable service, exploit it to gain code execution, copy the malware to the new host, and repeat, is a form of lateral movement (MITRE Tactic TA0008). When a worm performs the pivoting itself it is autonomous propagation; when human operators do it after an initial breach it is manual lateral movement.

The distinction from a virus matters: a virus requires a host file and typically user action, such as opening an attachment, to propagate. A worm needs neither, it finds and infects reachable hosts on its own, which is why worm outbreaks can escalate at machine speed.

A canonical propagation vector is Server Message Block (SMB), a Windows file-sharing and IPC protocol running over TCP port 445. Its complexity and long history of implementation bugs have made it a frequent target for remote code execution.

slides.title: Case Study: WannaCry, EternalBlue, and CVE-2017-0144

quiz.question: Using WannaCry as your example, (a) explain how a network worm differs mechanically from a DDoS attack, (b) identify the primary organizational failure that enabled WannaCry's global scale, and (c) name two technical controls that would have limited its spread.
quiz.prompt: Hint for (a): focus on code execution vs. resource exhaustion. For (b): recall when MS17-010 was released. For (c): think patch management, protocol deprecation, and internal segmentation/firewalling of port 445.
quiz.explanation: (a) A worm achieves actual remote code execution on the victim and self-replicates; WannaCry ran arbitrary code via EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144), installed DoublePulsar, dropped ransomware, then autonomously scanned for more SMB hosts. Availability loss (encrypted files) was a downstream side effect, not the direct mechanism. A DDoS never gains code execution, it merely exhausts a finite resource (bandwidth, connection state) to deny availability. (b) The primary failure was patch management: Microsoft released MS17-010 a full month before the outbreak, so vulnerable organizations had failed to apply an available fix. (c) Any two of: timely patch management (apply MS17-010); disable/deprecate SMBv1; restrict SMB/port 445 between internal segments at internal firewalls (segmentation); deploy IDS tuned to detect internal lateral scanning. Full credit requires the code-execution-vs-exhaustion distinction, naming patch management, and two valid controls.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Attributed by the U.S. and U.K. governments to North Korea's Lazarus Group. CVSS v3.0 base score 8.1 (High). Microsoft took the unusual step of patching out-of-support XP/Server 2003 after the outbreak began.

Misconception: That WannaCry was unstoppable/novel. The propagation vector was patchable a month earlier; the story is one of operational failure, not technical inevitability.

Worm vs. DoS: WannaCry achieved actual code execution and self-replicated; availability loss (encryption) was a side effect, not the primary mechanism as in a DDoS.

Exam tip: Be ready to classify a described scenario as worm vs. DoS by citing the mechanism (code execution + self-replication vs. resource exhaustion), and to name patch management as the primary organizational failure here.
bullets: May 2017: WannaCry ransomware worm hit 200,000+ computers across 150+ countries within days
Victims: U.K. National Health Service, Telefónica, FedEx, and many others
Exploit: EternalBlue, RCE in Microsoft's SMBv1 (CVE-2017-0144), leaked from the NSA by the Shadow Brokers
Chain: EternalBlue → DoublePulsar backdoor → ransomware payload → scan local /24 for more SMB hosts
Zero interaction: No user needed to click anything for the worm to spread host to host
Root cause: Patch MS17-010 shipped a full month earlier, this was a patch-management failure, not a zero-day

content_blocks: In May 2017, the WannaCry ransomware worm spread to over 200,000 computers across at least 150 countries within days, crippling parts of the U.K.'s National Health Service, Spain's Telefónica, and FedEx. WannaCry's propagation engine exploited EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144), a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft's legacy SMBv1 implementation, developed by the NSA and leaked by the Shadow Brokers in April 2017.

Once EternalBlue granted code execution with SYSTEM privileges, WannaCry installed the DoublePulsar kernel backdoor, dropped its ransomware payload, then scanned the local subnet for additional SMB-exposed hosts on TCP 445, repeating the exploit chain with no human operator at any stage. No user interaction occurred anywhere in the chain.

Critically, Microsoft had released patch MS17-010 for this exact vulnerability a full month before the outbreak. The devastating spread was therefore largely a story of failed patch management rather than a genuine zero-day surprise. The outbreak was slowed, not stopped, when researcher Marcus Hutchins registered an unregistered 'kill switch' domain hardcoded in the malware.

slides.title: Defense-in-Depth Across the Layers
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This synthesis slide maps each exploit family to its layer-appropriate control set. It sets up Topics 3.3 (segmentation), 3.4 (firewalls), and 3.5 (detection).

Misconception: That one silver-bullet product secures a network. Defense-in-depth exists precisely because each control has a narrow scope.

Analogy: A castle uses walls, a moat, gatehouses, and guards, not one enormous door. Each control covers a different avenue of attack.

Exam tip: When asked to defend against 'network-level exploits' broadly, name the layer AND the specific control for each threat family. Naming both is what separates full credit from partial.
bullets: No single control suffices: Sniffing, ARP spoofing, DoS, and worms each need different defenses
Layer 2: DAI + DHCP snooping, port security, VLAN segmentation, stop sniffing and on-path attacks
Layer 3/4: SYN cookies, BCP 38 ingress filtering, DDoS scrubbing, stop denial of service
Patch + deprecate: Apply updates promptly, disable SMBv1, restrict port 445 internally, stop worms
Segmentation as force multiplier: VLANs shrink the blast radius of any Layer 2 attack
Detection: IDS tuned for internal lateral scanning flags active worm propagation

content_blocks: Defense against network-level exploits requires controls at multiple layers of the stack, because no single control addresses sniffing, ARP spoofing, denial of service, and worm propagation simultaneously. The disciplined way to structure a defense, and a defense answer on the exam, is by OSI layer.

At Layer 2, Dynamic ARP Inspection with DHCP snooping, port security, and VLAN segmentation stop ARP-based sniffing and on-path attacks and contain their blast radius. At Layer 3/4, SYN cookies defeat protocol-state exhaustion, BCP 38 ingress filtering prevents spoofed-source packets, and DDoS scrubbing services absorb volumetric floods before they reach the origin. Above the network stack, timely patch management, deprecating legacy protocols like SMBv1, and restricting port 445 between internal segments stop worm propagation.

Segmentation is a force multiplier across all of these: by shrinking broadcast domains, it limits how far any single compromise can reach. Detection, an IDS tuned to spot anomalous internal scanning, provides the final safety net against an active worm.

slides.title: Detecting a SYN Flood from Captured Packets (Python)
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Real sensors parse live pcap via libraries like scapy or dpkt; here we use simple dictionaries so students focus on the heuristic, not the parsing API.

Misconception: That detection requires deep packet inspection. Simple flag-counting statistics catch many volumetric and protocol attacks.

Analogy: Counting how many people rang the doorbell but never came in, a spike in unanswered rings signals something is wrong.

Exam tip: Understand the SYN-to-ACK ratio as the detection signal. You will not code on the exam, but you may be asked what metric distinguishes a flood from normal traffic.
bullets: Signal: Many SYNs with few matching SYN-ACK completions from a single destination
Heuristic: Count SYN-only packets per source and per destination over a window
Half-open ratio: A high SYN-to-ACK ratio flags likely flooding
Spoofing hint: A huge count of distinct source IPs each sending a single SYN is suspicious
Practical use: Feed the count into an alerting threshold or IDS rule

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Real sensors parse live pcap via libraries like scapy or dpkt; here we use simple dictionaries so students focus on the heuristic, not the parsing API.

content_blocks: Detection turns raw packet data into actionable signal. The script below models the core SYN-flood heuristic: over a set of captured packets, it counts SYN-only segments (SYN set, ACK clear) per destination and compares them against completing ACKs. A destination receiving a large number of half-open SYNs relative to completed handshakes is a strong candidate for a SYN flood.

In a production IDS, this logic runs continuously over a sliding time window with a tuned threshold, and the diversity of source IPs is used as an additional signal, thousands of distinct sources each sending exactly one SYN is a hallmark of spoofed-source flooding. The example uses plain data structures so it runs anywhere, but the same logic underlies rules in Suricata and Snort.

slides.title: Detecting a SYN Flood from Captured Packets (Python)
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Real sensors parse live pcap via libraries like scapy or dpkt; here we use simple dictionaries so students focus on the heuristic, not the parsing API.

Misconception: That detection requires deep packet inspection. Simple flag-counting statistics catch many volumetric and protocol attacks.

Analogy: Counting how many people rang the doorbell but never came in, a spike in unanswered rings signals something is wrong.

Exam tip: Understand the SYN-to-ACK ratio as the detection signal. You will not code on the exam, but you may be asked what metric distinguishes a flood from normal traffic.

code_block.content:
# Simple SYN-flood heuristic over a list of captured packets.
# Each packet is a dict: {'src','dst','syn','ack'}
from collections import defaultdict

packets = [
    {'src': '203.0.113.44',  'dst': '198.51.100.10', 'syn': True,  'ack': False},
    {'src': '203.0.113.19',  'dst': '198.51.100.10', 'syn': True,  'ack': False},
    {'src': '198.51.100.201','dst': '198.51.100.10', 'syn': True,  'ack': False},
    {'src': '10.0.0.5',      'dst': '198.51.100.10', 'syn': True,  'ack': True},   # normal
]

syn_only = defaultdict(int)   # half-open attempts per destination
completed = defaultdict(int)  # handshakes with ACK per destination
sources = defaultdict(set)

for p in packets:
    if p['syn'] and not p['ack']:
        syn_only[p['dst']] += 1
        sources[p['dst']].add(p['src'])
    elif p['syn'] and p['ack']:
        completed[p['dst']] += 1

THRESHOLD = 2  # tuned per-window in production
for dst, half_open in syn_only.items():
    ratio = half_open / max(completed[dst], 1)
    if half_open >= THRESHOLD and ratio > 1:
        print(f'ALERT SYN flood -> {dst}: {half_open} half-open, '
              f'{len(sources[dst])} distinct sources, ratio {ratio:.1f}')

slides.title: Practice: Classifying Network Attacks

quiz.question: Employees on one office VLAN report that their HTTPS banking sessions are being intercepted in cleartext, and investigation shows their ARP caches all list the attacker's MAC as the default gateway. Which single control most directly prevents this attack at its root?
options: Enabling SYN cookies on the banking server
Deploying Dynamic ARP Inspection with DHCP snooping on the access switches
Contracting a DDoS scrubbing service
Applying the MS17-010 patch to all endpoints
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct. The scenario is ARP cache poisoning enabling an on-path SSL-stripping attack, a Layer 2 problem. Dynamic ARP Inspection, backed by a DHCP-snooping binding table, validates ARP claims and drops the forged gateway mappings at the switch, stopping the poisoning at its root. Option A defends against SYN floods (availability), not interception. Option C addresses volumetric DDoS. Option D patches the SMBv1 worm vector, unrelated to ARP poisoning. (HSTS would defend the SSL-stripping step specifically, but DAI prevents the on-path position that enables the whole attack.)

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This mirrors how AP scenario questions are graded, credit accrues for correct mechanism identification and a matching control, not for naming the symptom.

Misconception: That 'unavailable' always means DDoS. Worms, misconfiguration, and ransomware also cause outages via different mechanisms.

Analogy: A doctor diagnosing from mechanism (infection vs. injury) not just symptom (pain) prescribes the right treatment.

Exam tip: Build a mental table: attack -> layer -> resource/trust -> control. Populate it under time pressure and your answers will be complete.
bullets: Skill: Given a scenario, identify the exploit family, the OSI layer, and the correct countermeasure
Confidentiality threats: Sniffing, MAC flooding, ARP spoofing, SSL stripping
Availability threats: SYN flood (protocol), DNS/NTP amplification (volumetric), HTTP flood (application)
Propagation threats: Worms via unpatched network services (e.g., SMBv1)
Method: Name the mechanism, not just the symptom, that is what earns credit

Confidentiality attacks (sniffing, MAC flooding, ARP spoofing, SSL stripping) capture or alter data in transit. Availability attacks fall into volumetric, protocol, and application-layer DoS. Propagation attacks (worms) achieve code execution and self-replicate.

Work the quiz below by first identifying the exhausted resource or exploited trust assumption, then the OSI layer, then the layer-appropriate control. Resist matching on symptoms alone, 'the site went down' fits both a DDoS and a worm, so you must reason from the mechanism.

slides.title: What Sniffed Traffic Actually Exposes
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: DEF CON's 'Wall of Sheep' publicly displays credentials sniffed from attendees using cleartext protocols, a live demonstration of this exact risk.

Misconception: That HTTPS makes sniffing pointless. Metadata (SNI, DNS, timing, volume) survives encryption and can be highly revealing.

Analogy: Encryption seals the envelope, but the postmark, addresses, and package weight are still visible to anyone watching the mail.

Exam tip: Know which classic protocols are cleartext (HTTP/FTP/Telnet) versus their secure replacements (HTTPS/SFTP/SSH). This distinction appears frequently.
bullets: Cleartext protocols: HTTP, FTP, Telnet, POP3/IMAP, and SNMPv1/2c transmit credentials in the clear
Session tokens: Cookies captured mid-session enable session hijacking without a password
Metadata: Even encrypted traffic leaks endpoints, timing, sizes, and SNI/DNS lookups
Stream reassembly: Wireshark's 'Follow TCP Stream' rebuilds full conversations from captured packets
Credential harvesting: A single captured Telnet login yields a reusable administrative password

Misconception: That HTTPS makes sniffing pointless. Metadata (SNI, DNS, timing, volume) survives encryption and can be highly revealing.

content_blocks: The danger of sniffing is not the raw frames but what they carry. Legacy cleartext protocols, HTTP, FTP, Telnet, POP3/IMAP, SNMPv1/2c, transmit usernames and passwords with no encryption whatsoever. A single captured login can hand an attacker reusable administrative credentials.

Beyond passwords, session cookies are prime targets: capturing a valid session token lets an attacker impersonate a logged-in user without ever knowing the password, a technique called session hijacking. Wireshark's stream-reassembly features rebuild entire conversations, emails, web pages, file transfers, from the captured packet sequence.

Even when payloads are encrypted, traffic still leaks metadata: which hosts talk to which, when, how often, and how much. DNS queries and TLS SNI fields often reveal the destination site name in the clear, allowing surveillance even without decrypting content.

slides.title: Encryption: The Real Defeat of Passive Sniffing
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This slide reinforces the active/passive distinction, passive attacks are addressed by encryption and access control, not IDS.

Misconception: That a VPN makes you anonymous or invulnerable. A VPN protects traffic in transit across the untrusted segment; it does not fix endpoint compromise or application flaws.

Analogy: You cannot stop people from seeing you mail a letter, but a sealed, coded letter is safe even if intercepted.

Exam tip: For any 'defend against sniffing' prompt, lead with encryption. Detection-based answers score poorly against a purely passive adversary.
bullets: Principle: If captured traffic is encrypted end-to-end, sniffing yields ciphertext with no usable content
TLS/HTTPS: Protects web and API traffic; the modern default for all sensitive services
SSH: Replaces cleartext Telnet and rlogin for remote administration
VPN tunnels: Encrypt all traffic across an untrusted segment (e.g., public Wi-Fi)
Why encryption beats detection: Passive capture leaves no footprint to alert on, you cannot detect it, only render it useless

content_blocks: Because passive sniffing produces no detectable footprint, the correct primary defense is not detection but encryption. If the traffic an attacker captures is encrypted end-to-end, the capture yields only ciphertext, the confidentiality of the data survives even a total loss of physical medium security.

In practice this means TLS/HTTPS for web and API traffic, SSH in place of Telnet for remote administration, SFTP/SCP in place of FTP, and VPN tunnels to protect all traffic traversing an untrusted segment such as public Wi-Fi. Encryption transforms the sniffing problem from 'prevent all capture', which is nearly impossible on shared or wireless media, into 'ensure captured bytes are meaningless.'
This is a foundational security lesson: when you cannot prevent an adversary from observing, make observation worthless.

slides.title: Detecting ARP Spoofing
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: arpwatch predates DAI and remains useful on segments with unmanaged switches where DAI is unavailable.

Misconception: That static ARP entries are a complete solution. They defend one host and create maintenance burden; they are a stopgap, not an enterprise strategy.

Analogy: arpwatch is a neighbor who notices when the nameplate on the mailbox suddenly changes and calls to check.

Exam tip: Distinguish prevention (DAI, static entries) from detection (arpwatch, monitoring for duplicate MACs). Questions may ask for one specific category.
bullets: Duplicate MAC: The same MAC address suddenly claiming two different IPs (victim + gateway) is a red flag
Changed binding: A gateway IP whose MAC changes unexpectedly signals possible poisoning
Tools: arpwatch and XArp log and alert on IP-to-MAC binding changes over time
Traffic clue: A sudden burst of unsolicited ARP replies (gratuitous ARP) on the segment
Static entries: Hard-coding the gateway's MAC on critical hosts prevents override (but does not scale)

slides.title: Detecting ARP Spoofing
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: arpwatch predates DAI and remains useful on segments with unmanaged switches where DAI is unavailable.

Misconception: That static ARP entries are a complete solution. They defend one host and create maintenance burden; they are a stopgap, not an enterprise strategy.

Analogy: arpwatch is a neighbor who notices when the nameplate on the mailbox suddenly changes and calls to check.

content_blocks: While Dynamic ARP Inspection prevents poisoning at the switch, host- and monitor-level detection provides defense in depth. The classic tell-tale is a single MAC address suddenly bound to two IPs, typically the attacker's MAC claiming both the victim's and the gateway's addresses. Tools like arpwatch and XArp continuously record IP-to-MAC bindings and raise an alert whenever a binding changes unexpectedly, such as the default gateway's MAC suddenly changing.

Another signal is a burst of unsolicited (gratuitous) ARP replies on a segment where none is expected. On individual critical hosts, administrators can pin static ARP entries for the gateway so a forged reply cannot override the mapping, effective but operationally unscalable across a large fleet, which is why switch-level DAI is preferred for enterprise deployment.

slides.title: DNS Spoofing and Session Hijacking as On-Path Payloads
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: These are the 'active tampering' half of the man-in-the-middle threat, complementing passive logging.

Misconception: That stealing a session requires the password. A valid session token is often sufficient, which is why token protection matters as much as password strength.

Analogy: DNS spoofing is a corrupt directory-assistance operator giving you the wrong address; session hijacking is stealing your already-stamped entry wristband.

Exam tip: Pair each attack with its defense: DNS spoofing→DNSSEC, session hijacking→Secure/HttpOnly cookies + TLS.
bullets: Once on-path: An attacker can do more than watch, they can forge responses and steal sessions
DNS spoofing: Reply to a victim's DNS query with a forged IP, redirecting them to an attacker server
Session hijacking: Steal an active session cookie/token to impersonate the logged-in user
TCP hijacking: With visibility of sequence numbers, inject valid segments into an existing connection
Defense: DNSSEC signs DNS responses; Secure/HttpOnly cookies and TLS protect sessions

slides.title: DNS Spoofing and Session Hijacking as On-Path Payloads
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: These are the 'active tampering' half of the man-in-the-middle threat, complementing passive logging.

Misconception: That stealing a session requires the password. A valid session token is often sufficient, which is why token protection matters as much as password strength.

Analogy: DNS spoofing is a corrupt directory-assistance operator giving you the wrong address; session hijacking is stealing your already-stamped entry wristband.

Exam tip: Pair each attack with its defense: DNS spoofing→DNSSEC, session hijacking→Secure/HttpOnly cookies + TLS.
content_blocks: An on-path position obtained via ARP poisoning is a platform for several active follow-on attacks. In DNS spoofing, the attacker answers the victim's DNS query faster than the real resolver with a forged record, redirecting the victim to a malicious server while the address bar still shows the expected domain. In session hijacking, the attacker lifts an active session cookie from intercepted traffic and replays it to impersonate the authenticated user without ever learning the password. In classic TCP hijacking, an attacker who can observe sequence numbers injects crafted segments into an existing connection.

Defenses target each layer: DNSSEC cryptographically signs DNS records so forged responses are rejected; Secure and HttpOnly cookie flags plus end-to-end TLS keep session tokens encrypted and inaccessible to interception; and encryption in general denies the attacker the plaintext and sequence visibility these attacks require.

slides.title: DDoS: Why 'Distributed' Changes Everything
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The shift from DoS to DDoS in the late 1990s/2000s tracked the rise of large botnets. Today attacks routinely exceed hundreds of Gbps.

Misconception: That firewalls alone stop DDoS. On-premise firewalls sit behind the same saturated link and can themselves become the bottleneck; upstream scrubbing is required for volumetric floods.

Analogy: One heckler can be removed from a theater; ten thousand simultaneous hecklers scattered through the crowd cannot.

Exam tip: When a scenario says 'thousands of sources,' the answer involves upstream/cloud scrubbing and BCP 38, not simple IP blocking.
bullets: DoS vs. DDoS: DoS comes from one source; DDoS floods from thousands of coordinated sources
Botnet command: A C2 server directs compromised zombies to strike a single target simultaneously
Filtering is hard: You cannot simply block one IP, the traffic looks like it comes from everywhere
Attribution is hard: Real attackers hide behind the botnet and spoofed sources
Capacity asymmetry: Defenders must provision or rent more capacity than the aggregate attack

slides.title: DDoS: Why 'Distributed' Changes Everything
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The shift from DoS to DDoS in the late 1990s/2000s tracked the rise of large botnets. Today attacks routinely exceed hundreds of Gbps.

Misconception: That firewalls alone stop DDoS. On-premise firewalls sit behind the same saturated link and can themselves become the bottleneck; upstream scrubbing is required for volumetric floods.

Analogy: One heckler can be removed from a theater; ten thousand simultaneous hecklers scattered through the crowd cannot.

Exam tip: When a scenario says 'thousands of sources,' the answer involves upstream/cloud scrubbing and BCP 38, not simple IP blocking.
content_blocks: Why is a distributed denial-of-service attack so much harder to stop than a single-source one? Because distribution defeats the simplest defense: blocking the offending source. When traffic arrives from thousands of geographically dispersed, often legitimate-looking devices under botnet control, there is no single IP or subnet to filter, and much of the traffic is indistinguishable from real users at the packet level.

Distribution also frustrates attribution, the true operator hides behind a command-and-control server and a swarm of compromised zombies, while spoofed source addresses obscure origins further. Finally, DDoS imposes a capacity asymmetry: the defender must be able to absorb or scrub more traffic than the attacker can aggregate, which is why cloud-scale scrubbing services exist. The Mirai/Dyn attack embodied all three difficulties simultaneously.

slides.title: Low-and-Slow and Application-Layer Attacks
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Slowloris (2009) famously worked against Apache's threaded model. It illustrates that 'DoS' is about exhausting a specific finite resource, not necessarily bandwidth.

Misconception: That all DoS is high-volume. Low-and-slow attacks are the counterexample examiners like to use.

Analogy: Instead of jamming every checkout lane with a mob, a few people stand at each register slowly counting out pennies, blocking everyone behind them.

Exam tip: Match the DoS type to its exhausted resource: Slowloris→worker threads/connections, HTTP flood→CPU/DB, SYN flood→backlog memory, volumetric→bandwidth.
bullets: Slowloris: Opens many connections and sends partial HTTP headers slowly, holding server threads open
Low bandwidth, high impact: Exhausts the connection pool without saturating the link
HTTP flood: Many valid-looking requests for expensive dynamic pages exhaust CPU/database
Hard to filter: Requests are individually legitimate, no malformed packets to drop
Defense: Connection timeouts, per-client rate limits, reverse proxies, and WAFs

slides.title: Low-and-Slow and Application-Layer Attacks
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Slowloris (2009) famously worked against Apache's threaded model. It illustrates that 'DoS' is about exhausting a specific finite resource, not necessarily bandwidth.

content_blocks: Not every denial-of-service attack is a flood of raw volume. 'Low-and-slow' attacks like Slowloris open many connections to a web server and send HTTP headers a few bytes at a time, never completing the request. Each half-finished request ties up a server worker thread; with enough of them, the connection pool is exhausted and legitimate users cannot connect, all achieved with minimal bandwidth.

Application-layer HTTP floods take the opposite approach with individually valid requests, repeatedly hitting computationally expensive endpoints (search queries, report generation, login) to exhaust CPU, memory, or database capacity. Both are difficult to filter because the traffic is well-formed and looks like real usage. Defenses operate at the application tier: aggressive connection timeouts, per-client rate limiting, reverse proxies that buffer slow clients, and web application firewalls that fingerprint abusive behavior.

slides.title: Record-Breaking Amplification: Memcached and GitHub 2018
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The memcached vector was newly weaponized in early 2018 and quickly patched via vendor defaults disabling UDP. It reinforces the amplification lesson from the DNS/NTP slide with an extreme factor.

Misconception: That bigger attacks need fundamentally new defenses. The same principles, upstream scrubbing, disable open reflectors, BCP 38, apply regardless of scale.

Analogy: A whisper into a stadium PA system becomes a deafening roar; the fix is to lock the microphone away.

Exam tip: Use GitHub 2018 as the extreme amplification example and pair it with the same mitigations as DNS/NTP amplification.
bullets: February 2018: GitHub absorbed a 1.35 Tbps attack, then the largest ever recorded
Vector: Exposed memcached servers on UDP 11211 with an amplification factor up to ~51,000x
Mechanism: Tiny spoofed request → enormous cached response reflected at the victim
Mitigation: GitHub rerouted through Akamai Prolexic scrubbing within minutes
Root fix: Memcached should never be exposed to the internet; disable UDP; apply BCP 38

content_blocks: In February 2018, GitHub was struck by a 1.35 Tbps DDoS, at the time the largest ever publicly recorded. The vector was memcached amplification: thousands of misconfigured memcached caching servers, reachable on UDP port 11211, responded to tiny spoofed requests with cached payloads thousands of times larger, yielding amplification factors reported up to roughly 51,000x. A few gigabits of attacker traffic became a terabit-scale flood aimed at GitHub.

GitHub survived by rerouting its traffic through Akamai's Prolexic scrubbing infrastructure within minutes, which filtered the malicious volume upstream before it reached GitHub's origin. The root-cause fixes are unglamorous but decisive: memcached should never be exposed to the internet, its UDP interface should be disabled, and BCP 38 source-address validation prevents the spoofed requests that make reflection possible in the first place.

slides.title: A Short History of Network Worms
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SQL Slammer's UDP-based, single-packet design is why it spread at line rate, no handshake, no payload delivery delay. NotPetya (2017), though it looked like ransomware, was a destructive wiper attributed to state actors.

Misconception: That worms are a solved historical problem. The same pattern recurs whenever a new remotely exploitable service flaw meets slow patching.

Analogy: Each worm is a new strain exploiting whatever door was left unlocked that decade; the door changes, the burglary pattern does not.

Exam tip: You need not memorize every worm, but recognize the common thread: autonomous exploitation of an unpatched network service enabling exponential spread.
bullets: Morris Worm (1988): First major internet worm; exploited fingerd/sendmail; crashed ~10% of the early internet
Code Red (2001): Exploited IIS; defaced pages and launched DoS against the White House IP
SQL Slammer (2003): 376-byte UDP worm; doubled every ~8.5 seconds; saturated links worldwide in minutes
Conficker (2008): Exploited a Windows RPC flaw; built a resilient multi-million-host botnet
WannaCry/NotPetya (2017): Weaponized EternalBlue; ransomware/wiper payloads at global scale

slides.speaker_notes:

content_blocks: Network worms are not new, they are one of the oldest classes of malware, and their history illustrates the enduring pattern of exploiting a reachable, unpatched service. The 1988 Morris Worm, written by a graduate student, exploited flaws in fingerd and sendmail and inadvertently crashed a large fraction of the nascent internet, prompting the creation of the first CERT. Code Red (2001) exploited Microsoft IIS. SQL Slammer (2003), a mere 376-byte UDP payload, doubled its infected population roughly every 8.5 seconds and congested networks worldwide within minutes, the fastest-spreading worm in history.

Conficker (2008) exploited a Windows RPC vulnerability to assemble a resilient botnet of millions. WannaCry and NotPetya (2017) weaponized the leaked EternalBlue exploit. Across three decades the lesson is constant: a remotely exploitable, unpatched network service is a worm's runway, and speed of propagation consistently outpaces human response.

slides.title: The Worm Lifecycle and Containing Propagation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The discovery phase's scanning is the most detectable behavior, a single internal host suddenly probing hundreds of peers on one port is a hallmark IoC.

Misconception: That endpoint antivirus alone stops worms. AV may miss a novel worm; segmentation and patching remove the propagation surface entirely.

Analogy: A fire spreads by finding fuel (discovery) and igniting it (exploitation). Firebreaks (segmentation) and removing fuel (patching) stop the spread even if one room burns.

Exam tip: Map each containment control to the lifecycle phase it disrupts. This structured answer earns full marks on 'how would you limit worm spread' prompts.
bullets: 1. Target discovery: Scan address ranges for hosts running the vulnerable service/port
2. Exploitation: Trigger the remote vulnerability to gain code execution
3. Payload delivery: Copy the worm body and any secondary payload (backdoor, ransomware)
4. Propagation: From each new host, repeat discovery, exponential growth
Containment: Patch the service, segment the network, restrict the port internally, detect scanning

slides.title: The Worm Lifecycle and Containing Propagation
slides.speaker_notes:

content_blocks: Every network worm follows the same four-phase lifecycle: target discovery (scanning for reachable vulnerable hosts), exploitation (triggering the remote flaw to gain execution), payload delivery (copying itself plus any secondary payload), and propagation (each newly infected host restarting the cycle). Because every infected host becomes a new scanner, uncontained growth is exponential, which is why worms can span the globe in hours.

Containment attacks each phase. Patching removes the exploitable flaw, eliminating exploitation. Network segmentation and internal firewall rules restrict which hosts can even reach the vulnerable port (e.g., blocking SMB/445 between segments), throttling discovery and propagation. Intrusion detection tuned to spot the anomalous internal scanning of the discovery phase provides early warning regardless of the specific exploit. No single measure is sufficient; together they break the exponential chain.

slides.title: Ingress and Egress Filtering (BCP 38 in Practice)
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: BCP 38 is a 'tragedy of the commons' problem, each operator bears a small cost, and the benefit accrues to the whole internet, so adoption lags.

Misconception: That filtering is only about inbound protection. Egress filtering protects everyone else from your network and catches internal compromise.

Analogy: A post office refusing to mail letters with obviously fake return addresses prevents its customers from framing others.

Exam tip: Associate amplification/reflection defense with egress filtering / BCP 38 at the source network, not just filtering at the victim.
bullets: Ingress filtering: Drop inbound packets whose source addresses could not legitimately originate from that direction
Egress filtering: Drop outbound packets whose source is not a valid internal address, stops your network spoofing others
BCP 38 / RFC 2827: The best-practice standard mandating source-address validation at the edge
Anti-spoofing payoff: Universally deployed, it would eliminate reflection/amplification DDoS
Bonus: Egress filtering also flags compromised internal hosts attempting to spoof or exfiltrate

slides.title: Ingress and Egress Filtering (BCP 38 in Practice)
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: BCP 38 is a 'tragedy of the commons' problem, each operator bears a small cost, and the benefit accrues to the whole internet, so adoption lags.

Misconception: That filtering is only about inbound protection. Egress filtering protects everyone else from your network and catches internal compromise.

Analogy: A post office refusing to mail letters with obviously fake return addresses prevents its customers from framing others.

Exam tip: Associate amplification/reflection defense with egress filtering / BCP 38 at the source network, not just filtering at the victim.
content_blocks: Source-address validation is one of the highest-leverage yet under-deployed network defenses. Ingress filtering drops inbound packets whose claimed source address could not legitimately arrive on that interface. Egress filtering, arguably more important for good internet citizenship, drops outbound packets whose source is not a valid address from inside your own network, preventing your hosts from spoofing others.

Codified as BCP 38 (RFC 2827), egress source-address validation directly disables the spoofed-source packets that reflection and amplification DDoS attacks depend on. If every network operator enforced it, spoofing-based attacks would largely vanish; incomplete adoption is precisely why they persist. As a bonus, egress filtering surfaces compromised internal machines attempting to spoof source addresses or exfiltrate data, doubling as a detection signal.

slides.title: Managerial Controls: Policy, Patching, and IoT Governance
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The AP framework explicitly values managerial (administrative) controls alongside technical ones. Both Dyn and WannaCry are teaching vehicles for policy lessons.

Misconception: That security is purely a technical problem. Most large breaches trace to process failures, unpatched systems, unknown assets, unrehearsed response.

Analogy: A fire suppression system (technical) is useless without inspection schedules, evacuation drills, and an emergency plan (managerial).

Exam tip: When asked for defenses, include at least one managerial control (patch policy, asset inventory, IR plan). Answers that mix technical and administrative controls score highest.
bullets: Patch management policy: Defined SLAs for applying critical updates (WannaCry proved the cost of delay)
Asset inventory: You cannot patch or segment what you do not know exists, especially IoT
Default-credential prohibition: Enforce credential changes on deployment (echoing California SB-327)
Vendor/supply-chain review: Assess third-party dependencies (Dyn showed single-point-of-failure risk)
Incident response plan: Predefined DDoS and worm playbooks shorten time-to-mitigation

content_blocks: Technical controls operate inside a managerial framework, and the case studies in this topic are as much governance failures as technical ones. WannaCry was fundamentally a patch-management failure; Mirai/Dyn exposed default-credential and supply-chain dependency risks. Accordingly, a mature program defines patch-management SLAs that require critical updates within a bounded window, maintains an accurate asset inventory (you cannot patch or segment unknown devices, and IoT is the usual blind spot), and prohibits deployment of devices with default credentials, the same principle California codified in SB-327.

Governance also demands supply-chain and vendor risk review, because outsourced dependencies like DNS can become single points of failure, and predefined incident-response playbooks for DDoS and worm outbreaks so that engaging a scrubbing service or isolating a segment is a rehearsed action rather than an improvised scramble. Managerial and technical controls reinforce each other; neither suffices alone.

slides.title: Practice: DoS Attack Type Identification

quiz.question: A service remains reachable at normal bandwidth, but its web workers are all stuck handling connections that send HTTP headers one byte at a time and never finish. Legitimate users get timeouts. What is the attack and its best mitigation?
options: Volumetric flood; mitigate with upstream DDoS scrubbing
SYN flood; mitigate with SYN cookies
Slowloris-style low-and-slow attack; mitigate with connection timeouts and a buffering reverse proxy
DNS amplification; mitigate with BCP 38 egress filtering
quiz.explanation: Option C is correct. Partial, never-completing HTTP requests that hold worker threads open at low bandwidth are the signature of a Slowloris-style low-and-slow attack; the exhausted resource is the connection/worker pool. Aggressive connection timeouts and a reverse proxy that buffers slow clients are the direct mitigations. Option A misreads it as volumetric (bandwidth is normal). Option B targets TCP backlog, but the handshake here completes, the abuse is at the HTTP layer. Option D is a reflection attack, not what is described.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This consolidates the DoS slides into a repeatable decision procedure students can apply under exam time pressure.

Misconception: That the biggest number always means volumetric. A small packet-per-second SYN flood can be as crippling as a large bandwidth flood, via a different resource.

Analogy: A triage nurse classifies by symptom pattern before treating; misclassification wastes the wrong resource.

Exam tip: Always state the exhausted resource explicitly, it is the fastest route to the correct classification and control.
bullets: Signal 1, resource: Is bandwidth, connection state, worker threads, or CPU/DB being exhausted?
Signal 2, volume: High-throughput flood vs. low-and-slow trickle vs. valid-looking requests
Signal 3, sources: One source, a botnet swarm, or reflected off third parties
Map to type: volumetric / protocol / application-layer / reflection-amplification
Then choose control: scrubbing / SYN cookies / rate limiting / BCP 38
