slides.title: Anatomy of a Packet: Headers Attackers Forge
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This foundational slide grounds later attacks. TTL, for instance, can reveal OS fingerprints and detect spoofing; flag combinations define scan types.

Misconception: That headers are immutable protocol plumbing. They are attacker-controllable data; the network trusts them by default.

Analogy: A packet is nested envelopes, each layer's envelope has an address label anyone can rewrite before mailing.

Exam tip: Be able to place a field at its layer (MAC=L2, IP=L3, port/flags=L4) and name which attack abuses it.
bullets: Encapsulation: Application data is wrapped in TCP/UDP, then IP, then an Ethernet frame, each layer adds a header
Ethernet header (L2): Source/destination MAC, trivially spoofable in software
IP header (L3): Source/destination IP, TTL, protocol, source IP spoofable on connectionless UDP
TCP header (L4): Ports, sequence/ack numbers, flags (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST)
Why it matters: Nearly every network attack forges or abuses a specific header field

slides.speaker_notes:

content_blocks: To understand network exploits at a mechanical level, you must understand how data is packaged. Encapsulation wraps application data in successive headers: a TCP or UDP header (Layer 4, carrying ports and, for TCP, sequence/acknowledgment numbers and control flags), an IP header (Layer 3, carrying source and destination IP addresses, TTL, and protocol), and finally an Ethernet frame header (Layer 2, carrying source and destination MAC addresses).

Each field is a potential lever. MAC addresses are trivially spoofable in software (enabling ARP spoofing and MAC spoofing). Source IP addresses can be forged on connectionless UDP (enabling reflection/amplification). TCP flags define the handshake a SYN flood abuses, and sequence numbers are what a hijacker must predict. Reading these headers, in Wireshark or tcpdump, is the core forensic skill of this unit, because the attack is almost always visible as an anomaly in a specific field.

slides.title: Port Scanning and Network Reconnaissance
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: nmap is the canonical scanner. The same activity is legitimate for defenders (vulnerability assessment) and malicious for attackers, context and authorization distinguish them.

Misconception: That a closed port and a filtered port are the same. Closed = host reachable but nothing listening (RST); filtered = firewall dropping probes (no reply). The distinction reveals firewall placement.

Analogy: A burglar walking down a hallway trying every doorknob and noting which are locked, unlocked, or walled off.

Exam tip: Know SYN-ACK=open, RST=closed, no-response=filtered. Scanning is the recon step preceding exploitation and the discovery phase of worms.
bullets: Reconnaissance: Before exploitation, attackers map which hosts exist and which services they run
Port scan: Probe TCP/UDP ports to discover open, closed, or filtered services (e.g., nmap)
SYN scan: Send SYN, infer state from SYN-ACK (open) vs RST (closed), never completing the handshake ('half-open')
Service/version detection: Banner grabbing reveals software versions to match against known CVEs
Detection: A single source touching many ports/hosts quickly is a classic IDS signature

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: nmap is the canonical scanner. The same activity is legitimate for defenders (vulnerability assessment) and malicious for attackers, context and authorization distinguish them.

Misconception: That a closed port and a filtered port are the same. Closed = host reachable but nothing listening (RST); filtered = firewall dropping probes (no reply). The distinction reveals firewall placement.

Analogy: A burglar walking down a hallway trying every doorknob and noting which are locked, unlocked, or walled off.

content_blocks: Exploitation is preceded by reconnaissance: the attacker must learn which hosts are alive and which services they expose. Port scanning is the primary tool. A scanner such as nmap probes a range of TCP or UDP ports and classifies each as open, closed, or filtered based on the responses. A TCP SYN ('half-open') scan sends a SYN and infers the port state from the reply, a SYN-ACK means open, a RST means closed, and silence often means a firewall is filtering, without ever completing the handshake, making it faster and stealthier than a full connect scan.

Beyond discovering open ports, service and version detection (banner grabbing) identifies the exact software and version behind a port, which the attacker cross-references against known CVEs to select an exploit. This is exactly the discovery phase a worm automates. Because scanning produces a distinctive pattern, one source rapidly touching many ports or many hosts, it is one of the most reliably detectable precursor behaviors for an IDS.

slides.title: MAC Spoofing and Its Limits
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: MAC filtering on home Wi-Fi is a classic example of security theater, it deters casual users but not an attacker who can sniff a valid MAC and clone it.

Misconception: That MAC allow-lists provide meaningful access control. They provide almost none against a capable adversary.

Analogy: A club that admits anyone wearing a specific color wristband, trivial to counterfeit once you see one.

Exam tip: When a scenario relies on MAC filtering for security, the correct critique is that MACs are spoofable; the fix is 802.1X (previewed here, detailed in 3.2).
bullets: MAC spoofing: Software-changing a NIC's source MAC to impersonate another device or evade filters
Uses: Bypass MAC-based access control, defeat MAC allow-lists, or masquerade after port security learns a MAC
Trivial to do: One command (ip link set eth0 address ..), MAC is not a security credential
Limit, Layer 2 only: Like ARP attacks, confined to the local segment
Defense: 802.1X port authentication ties access to credentials, not to a forgeable MAC

slides.title: MAC Spoofing and Its Limits
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: MAC filtering on home Wi-Fi is a classic example of security theater, it deters casual users but not an attacker who can sniff a valid MAC and clone it.

Misconception: That MAC allow-lists provide meaningful access control. They provide almost none against a capable adversary.

Analogy: A club that admits anyone wearing a specific color wristband, trivial to counterfeit once you see one.

Exam tip: When a scenario relies on MAC filtering for security, the correct critique is that MACs are spoofable; the fix is 802.1X (previewed here, detailed in 3.2).
content_blocks: A MAC address is a hardware identifier, but it is not a security credential, it can be changed in software with a single command. MAC spoofing sets a NIC's source MAC to an arbitrary value, letting an attacker impersonate another device, bypass MAC-based access control lists (common on Wi-Fi and captive portals), or masquerade as a device that port security has already learned and authorized.

The limitation mirrors other Layer 2 attacks: MAC spoofing only affects the local segment. Its real lesson is architectural, any control that trusts a MAC address as proof of identity is fundamentally weak, because the identifier is attacker-controlled. The robust replacement is 802.1X port-based network access control, which requires a device to authenticate with real credentials (via a RADIUS server) before the switch port forwards any traffic, binding access to something that cannot be trivially forged.

slides.title: Deep Question: Why Not Just Authenticate ARP?
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This mirrors a recurring theme: fixing a protocol in place is often infeasible, so defenses migrate to a chokepoint (the switch, the resolver, the browser).

Misconception: That insecure protocols persist out of ignorance. They persist because backward compatibility and deployment inertia are enormous forces.

Analogy: Rather than reissuing every citizen a new ID card overnight, you install verification scanners at the doors that matter.

Exam tip: Use this reasoning for any 'why not just fix the protocol?' question, cite deployment inertia, backward compatibility, and cost, then point to infrastructure-side mitigation.
bullets: The obvious fix: Cryptographically sign ARP replies so forgeries are rejected
S-ARP proposal: Research designs added public-key signatures to ARP, but never saw wide deployment
Cost barrier: Per-packet crypto and a key-distribution/PKI burden on a chatty broadcast protocol
Backward compatibility: The entire installed base speaks unauthenticated ARP; a flag day is impossible
Pragmatic answer: Push validation into the switch (DAI) instead of changing every host's protocol

slides.title: Deep Question: Why Not Just Authenticate ARP?
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This mirrors a recurring theme: fixing a protocol in place is often infeasible, so defenses migrate to a chokepoint (the switch, the resolver, the browser).

Misconception: That insecure protocols persist out of ignorance. They persist because backward compatibility and deployment inertia are enormous forces.

Analogy: Rather than reissuing every citizen a new ID card overnight, you install verification scanners at the doors that matter.

Exam tip: Use this reasoning for any 'why not just fix the protocol?' question, cite deployment inertia, backward compatibility, and cost, then point to infrastructure-side mitigation.
content_blocks: If ARP's flaw is that it is unauthenticated, why not simply add authentication? Researchers did propose exactly this, Secure ARP (S-ARP) and similar schemes attach public-key signatures to ARP messages so a host can verify a reply genuinely came from the claimed IP's owner. The idea is sound, yet none achieved broad deployment, and the reasons are instructive about real-world security engineering.

First, cost: signing and verifying every ARP message imposes cryptographic overhead on an extremely chatty, latency-sensitive broadcast protocol, and it requires a key-distribution or PKI mechanism that ARP was never designed to carry. Second, backward compatibility: the entire installed base of operating systems and devices speaks plain, unauthenticated ARP, and there is no feasible 'flag day' to upgrade the world at once. The pragmatic resolution was to leave the host protocol untouched and instead push validation into the infrastructure, Dynamic ARP Inspection at the switch, where a single upgrade protects many unmodified hosts.

slides.title: TCP Reset Attacks and Connection Tampering
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The BGP reset threat motivated TCP-AO / MD5 signatures on BGP sessions. Great Firewall-style censorship has historically used injected RSTs.

Misconception: That RST injection needs full traffic capture. On-path it is trivial; off-path it only needs an in-window sequence guess, which is why sequence randomization matters.

Analogy: Slipping a forged 'meeting cancelled' note that looks official enough to end a conversation instantly.

Exam tip: Connect RST attacks to the value of sequence-number randomization and to encryption/integrity as the general defense against on-path tampering.
bullets: RST flag: A TCP segment with RST set immediately tears down a connection
Reset attack: An attacker who can guess/observe the sequence number injects a forged RST to kill a session
Requirements: Correct source/dest IPs and ports plus an in-window sequence number
Uses: Censorship (severing connections), disrupting long-lived sessions (BGP, SSH)
Defense: Encryption/integrity (TLS, IPsec) and larger sequence spaces make injection impractical

Context: The BGP reset threat motivated TCP-AO / MD5 signatures on BGP sessions. Great Firewall-style censorship has historically used injected RSTs.

Misconception: That RST injection needs full traffic capture. On-path it is trivial; off-path it only needs an in-window sequence guess, which is why sequence randomization matters.

content_blocks: The TCP RST (reset) flag exists to abruptly terminate a connection, for example when a segment arrives for a socket that no longer exists. An attacker can weaponize it: by forging a segment with the correct source and destination IPs and ports and a sequence number that falls within the receiver's current window, they can inject a spurious RST that tears down a legitimate connection. This is a TCP reset attack, a targeted denial of a specific session rather than a flood.

An on-path attacker who directly observes the sequence numbers can do this reliably; even an off-path attacker can sometimes succeed by guessing within the window. Reset attacks have been used for network censorship (severing prohibited connections) and to disrupt long-lived sessions like BGP peerings or SSH. The defenses are the familiar ones: end-to-end integrity and encryption (TLS, IPsec) prevent an attacker from crafting an accepted segment, and modern large, randomized sequence spaces make blind guessing impractical.

slides.title: ICMP-Based Attacks: Smurf and Ping Floods
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Smurf is the conceptual ancestor of DNS/NTP/memcached amplification, same spoofed-source reflection idea, different reflector. The historical fix (no directed broadcasts) is why it faded.

Misconception: That blocking all ICMP is the right answer. ICMP is operationally important (path MTU discovery); the fix is disabling directed broadcasts and rate limiting, not blanket blocking.

Analogy: Shouting a question into a crowded room with someone else's name attached, so the whole room answers that person.

Exam tip: Recognize Smurf as reflection/amplification and name 'disable directed broadcasts + BCP 38' as the fix. Note the family resemblance to DNS amplification.
bullets: ICMP: The control/diagnostic protocol behind ping and traceroute
Ping flood: Overwhelm a target with ICMP Echo Requests (crude volumetric DoS)
Smurf attack: Send ICMP Echo to a network's broadcast address with the victim's IP spoofed as source
Amplification: Every host on that network replies to the victim, an early reflection technique
Defense: Disable directed broadcasts (RFC 2644), rate-limit ICMP, and apply BCP 38

content_blocks: ICMP, the Internet Control Message Protocol, powers diagnostics like ping and traceroute, and has historically been abused for denial of service. A ping flood is the crudest form: overwhelm a target with a high rate of ICMP Echo Requests. More elegant is the Smurf attack, an early reflection/amplification technique. The attacker sends ICMP Echo Requests to a network's broadcast address while spoofing the victim's IP as the source. Every host on that network dutifully replies to the victim, so a single spoofed packet elicits dozens or hundreds of responses converging on the target.

Smurf attacks were devastating in the late 1990s and are now largely historical because the fix was decisive: RFC 2644 changed the default so routers no longer forward directed broadcasts, eliminating the amplifier. Together with ICMP rate limiting and BCP 38 source-address validation, this closed the vector, a clean example of a protocol default change neutralizing an entire attack class.

slides.title: Rogue DHCP and DHCP Starvation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This shows DHCP snooping's dual value, it both stops rogue DHCP and provides the binding table for DAI. One control, two threats.

Misconception: That on-path attacks require ARP poisoning. Rogue DHCP achieves the same gateway redirection through a different unauthenticated protocol.

Analogy: An imposter concierge who hands newly-arrived guests a fake building directory listing themselves as the front desk.

Exam tip: Link DHCP snooping to both rogue-DHCP prevention and DAI's binding table. Recognize rogue DHCP as an alternative route to an on-path position.
bullets: DHCP starvation: Flood DHCP requests with spoofed MACs to exhaust the server's address pool
Effect: Legitimate clients cannot obtain a lease, a denial of service on address assignment
Rogue DHCP server: Attacker's server answers first, handing out a malicious gateway/DNS
Outcome: Victims route through the attacker (on-path) or resolve to malicious DNS
Defense: DHCP snooping designates trusted server ports and blocks rogue server replies

slides.title: Rogue DHCP and DHCP Starvation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This shows DHCP snooping's dual value, it both stops rogue DHCP and provides the binding table for DAI. One control, two threats.

Misconception: That on-path attacks require ARP poisoning. Rogue DHCP achieves the same gateway redirection through a different unauthenticated protocol.

content_blocks: DHCP, which automatically assigns IP configuration to hosts, is another unauthenticated Layer 2 service ripe for abuse. In DHCP starvation, the attacker floods the legitimate DHCP server with requests bearing spoofed MAC addresses, exhausting its finite pool of leasable addresses so real clients can no longer obtain configuration, a denial of service on the address-assignment function itself.

The starvation is often a setup for the more dangerous rogue DHCP server attack: with the real server unable to respond, the attacker stands up their own DHCP server that answers clients first, handing out an IP configuration that points the victim's default gateway and DNS server at the attacker. The result is an on-path position (all traffic routed through the attacker) and/or DNS redirection, achieved without touching ARP at all.

The defense is DHCP snooping, the same feature that underpins Dynamic ARP Inspection: it marks only legitimate server ports as trusted and drops DHCP server messages arriving on untrusted (end-host) ports.

slides.title: Botnets and Command-and-Control
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The kill-switch domain in WannaCry and takedowns of botnets like Emotet illustrate the leverage of C2 disruption.

Misconception: That every infected device must be cleaned to stop a botnet. Disrupting C2 can be sufficient to render the swarm inert.

Analogy: An army of puppets is only dangerous while the puppeteer can pull the strings, cut the strings (C2) and it collapses.

Exam tip: Know that botnets power DDoS and that C2 disruption is the primary takedown strategy. Recognize P2P C2 as the resilient, harder-to-kill design.
bullets: Botnet: A network of compromised devices ('zombies') under unified attacker control
Command-and-control (C2): The channel through which the operator issues orders to the swarm
C2 architectures: Centralized (single server), tiered (proxies), or peer-to-peer (resilient, no single point)
Uses: DDoS floods, spam, credential stuffing, crypto-mining, malware distribution
Takedown lever: Seizing or sinkholing C2 infrastructure disrupts the whole botnet

slides.title: Botnets and Command-and-Control
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The kill-switch domain in WannaCry and takedowns of botnets like Emotet illustrate the leverage of C2 disruption.

Misconception: That every infected device must be cleaned to stop a botnet. Disrupting C2 can be sufficient to render the swarm inert.

content_blocks: A botnet is a network of compromised, internet-connected devices, a 'zombie army', under the unified command of an attacker. The devices are recruited by malware that scans for and exploits weak credentials or vulnerable services (Mirai's model), and each awaits instructions over a command-and-control (C2) channel. C2 architectures vary in resilience: a simple centralized server is easy to operate but easy to take down; tiered designs interpose proxies; peer-to-peer botnets like later Conficker variants have no single point of failure, making them far harder to dismantle.

Botnets are the engine behind large-scale abuse: volumetric DDoS floods, spam campaigns, credential-stuffing attacks, crypto-mining, and malware distribution, all executed at massive scale by coordinating thousands of hosts. Because the C2 channel is the botnet's nervous system, defenders and law enforcement prioritize identifying and sinkholing or seizing C2 infrastructure, which can neutralize the entire swarm even without cleaning individual infected devices.

slides.title: Case Study: NotPetya (2017), When a Worm Is a Weapon
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NotPetya was attributed to Russian military actors targeting Ukraine, with global collateral damage. It is the canonical supply-chain + lateral-movement worm case, complementing WannaCry's patch-management lesson.

Misconception: That patching alone would have stopped it. Patched machines still fell via stolen credentials and PsExec, showing why segmentation and least privilege matter beyond patching.

Analogy: A burglar who enters through a trusted delivery service, then uses the building's own master keys (stolen credentials) to open every door.

Exam tip: Contrast NotPetya (supply-chain entry, multi-technique lateral movement, wiper) with WannaCry (single SMB exploit, ransomware, kill switch). Both argue for segmentation and least privilege.
bullets: June 2017: NotPetya spread from a compromised Ukrainian accounting-software update (M.E.Doc)
Propagation: Combined EternalBlue with credential theft (Mimikatz) and PsExec/WMI for lateral movement
Disguise: Looked like ransomware but was a wiper, encryption was irreversible by design
Damage: ~$10 billion globally; Maersk, Merck, and FedEx/TNT crippled
Lesson: Supply-chain compromise + aggressive lateral movement defeats a hard perimeter

slides.title: Case Study: NotPetya (2017), When a Worm Is a Weapon
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NotPetya was attributed to Russian military actors targeting Ukraine, with global collateral damage. It is the canonical supply-chain + lateral-movement worm case, complementing WannaCry's patch-management lesson.

Misconception: That patching alone would have stopped it. Patched machines still fell via stolen credentials and PsExec, showing why segmentation and least privilege matter beyond patching.

Analogy: A burglar who enters through a trusted delivery service, then uses the building's own master keys (stolen credentials) to open every door.

Exam tip: Contrast NotPetya (supply-chain entry, multi-technique lateral movement, wiper) with WannaCry (single SMB exploit, ransomware, kill switch). Both argue for segmentation and least privilege.
content_blocks: NotPetya, which erupted in June 2017 just weeks after WannaCry, demonstrates a more sophisticated and destructive worm. Its initial vector was a supply-chain compromise: attackers backdoored the update mechanism of M.E.Doc, a Ukrainian accounting package, pushing the malware to organizations that trusted a legitimate software update. Once inside, NotPetya did not rely on EternalBlue alone, it combined the SMB exploit with credential theft (Mimikatz-style harvesting of in-memory passwords) and legitimate administration tools (PsExec, WMI) to move laterally even to fully patched machines using stolen valid credentials.

Though it displayed a ransom note, NotPetya was effectively a wiper: its encryption was irreversible by design, so paying accomplished nothing. Estimated global damage reached roughly $10 billion, crippling shipping giant Maersk, pharmaceutical company Merck, and FedEx's TNT unit. The enduring lesson is that a hard perimeter is no defense against a threat that enters through a trusted supply chain and then spreads using valid credentials and built-in tools, motivating segmentation, credential hygiene, and least privilege.

slides.title: Getting Visibility: TAPs, SPAN, and Sensor Placement
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This slide bridges 3.1's threats to 3.5's detection by establishing how sensors get their data. East-west visibility is a recurring enterprise gap.

Misconception: That a perimeter sensor sees internal lateral movement. It does not, traffic between two internal hosts never crosses the perimeter, so east-west sensors or TAPs are required.

Analogy: Security cameras only in the lobby miss everything happening between offices upstairs.

Exam tip: Distinguish north-south (perimeter) from east-west (internal) monitoring, and know TAPs are lossless while SPAN can drop under load.
bullets: You can't defend what you can't see: Detection requires a legitimate copy of traffic
SPAN/port mirroring: Switch copies traffic to a monitor port, flexible but can drop under load
Network TAP: A passive hardware device that copies traffic on the wire, reliable, no packet loss
Placement: At perimeter (north-south) and between segments (east-west) for internal visibility
Feeds: IDS/IPS sensors, packet capture, and NetFlow collectors (detailed in Topic 3.5)

slides.title: Getting Visibility: TAPs, SPAN, and Sensor Placement
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This slide bridges 3.1's threats to 3.5's detection by establishing how sensors get their data. East-west visibility is a recurring enterprise gap.

Misconception: That a perimeter sensor sees internal lateral movement. It does not, traffic between two internal hosts never crosses the perimeter, so east-west sensors or TAPs are required.

Analogy: Security cameras only in the lobby miss everything happening between offices upstairs.

Exam tip: Distinguish north-south (perimeter) from east-west (internal) monitoring, and know TAPs are lossless while SPAN can drop under load.
content_blocks: Every detection capability in Topic 3.5 depends on first obtaining a faithful copy of network traffic, legitimately. Two mechanisms dominate. SPAN (port mirroring) configures the switch to copy traffic from source ports or VLANs to a monitoring port; it is flexible and requires no extra hardware, but under heavy load a switch may drop mirrored packets, silently blinding the sensor. A network TAP is a dedicated passive device inserted in-line on a physical link that copies every bit to a monitoring port with no risk of loss and no impact on the production path, the gold standard for forensic-grade capture.

Placement matters as much as method. Sensors at the perimeter observe north-south traffic (in/out of the organization), while sensors between internal segments observe east-west traffic, exactly where lateral movement and worm propagation occur but where visibility is often weakest. This visibility architecture is the physical foundation for the IDS/IPS and log analysis covered in Topic 3.5.

slides.title: Practice: Reading a Packet Capture for Indicators

quiz.question: In a capture, you observe a single internal IP sending TCP SYN packets to destination ports 21, 22, 23, 25, 80, 110, 143, 443, and 445 on twenty different hosts within two seconds, receiving a mix of SYN-ACK and RST replies. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: A SYN flood denial-of-service attack against those twenty hosts
A port/host scan performing network reconnaissance and service discovery
Normal web browsing generating background traffic
An ARP cache poisoning attack in progress
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct. One source rapidly probing many well-known service ports across many hosts, and interpreting SYN-ACK (open) vs RST (closed) replies, is the signature of a port/host scan for reconnaissance, the discovery phase before exploitation. Option A is wrong: a SYN flood targets one victim with a huge SYN volume and no interest in the replies, not a sweep across many ports/hosts. Option C is wrong: browsing does not systematically walk service ports. Option D is wrong: ARP poisoning involves forged ARP replies at Layer 2, not TCP SYNs to service ports.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This operationalizes the header-anatomy and detection slides. Real analysts live in display filters; students should recognize the signature patterns even without tool fluency.

Misconception: That you must inspect every packet. You form a hypothesis and filter to it, capture analysis is targeted, not exhaustive.

Analogy: A detective does not read every page of every file, they search for the specific fingerprint that confirms a theory.

Exam tip: Match each anomaly pattern to its attack: duplicate MAC→ARP poisoning, SYN-heavy→SYN flood, many-ports-one-source→scan, cleartext creds→protocol risk.
bullets: ARP anomaly: One MAC bound to multiple IPs, or the gateway MAC changing → ARP poisoning
SYN anomaly: Many SYNs, few completed handshakes, many source IPs → SYN flood
Scan anomaly: One source touching many ports/hosts in sequence → reconnaissance
Cleartext credentials: Basic-auth or FTP USER/PASS visible → cleartext-protocol risk
Method: Filter, then interpret the pattern against a known attack signature

content_blocks: Reading a capture is pattern recognition against known signatures. In Wireshark you filter to isolate a hypothesis, then interpret: arp.duplicate-address-detected or a gateway MAC that changes mid-capture indicates ARP poisoning; a flood of tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0 with almost no completing ACKs and a huge spread of source IPs indicates a SYN flood; one internal source hitting many destination ports in ascending order indicates a port scan; and visible http.authorization or FTP USER/PASS commands indicate credentials traversing a cleartext protocol.

The discipline is always the same: form a hypothesis about the attack, apply a display filter that would confirm or refute it, and read the resulting pattern. The quiz below exercises this reasoning against a described capture.

slides.title: Topic 3.1 Synthesis and Bridge to Segmentation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This bridge slide connects 3.1's exploit families to the defensive topics that follow (segmentation, firewalls, detection) and to the wireless-specific escalation in 3.2.

Misconception: That wired and wireless threats are wholly separate. Most wireless attacks are the same on-path/sniffing concepts amplified by the absence of physical containment.

Analogy: Wired networks are conversations inside a building; wireless broadcasts them into the street where anyone nearby can listen.

Exam tip: Keep the CIA framing handy, the exam often asks which property (confidentiality, integrity, availability) a given attack primarily threatens.
bullets: Unifying theme: Legacy protocols trust the wire; attackers weaponize that trust at whatever layer they can reach
Confidentiality: Sniffing and ARP-based on-path attacks, defeated by encryption + Layer 2 hardening
Availability: SYN floods and amplification, defeated by SYN cookies, BCP 38, and scrubbing
Propagation: Worms over unpatched services, defeated by patching, deprecation, and internal firewalling
Blast radius: Every attack here is smaller when the network is well segmented
Next: Topic 3.2 extends these threats to the uniquely exposed wireless medium

slides.title: Topic 3.1 Synthesis and Bridge to Segmentation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This bridge slide connects 3.1's exploit families to the defensive topics that follow (segmentation, firewalls, detection) and to the wireless-specific escalation in 3.2.

Misconception: That wired and wireless threats are wholly separate. Most wireless attacks are the same on-path/sniffing concepts amplified by the absence of physical containment.

Analogy: Wired networks are conversations inside a building; wireless broadcasts them into the street where anyone nearby can listen.

Exam tip: Keep the CIA framing handy, the exam often asks which property (confidentiality, integrity, availability) a given attack primarily threatens.
content_blocks: Topic 3.1 established the threat landscape of the network fabric. The recurring theme is that foundational protocols were designed to trust any participant on the wire, and attackers exploit that trust at the lowest layer they can physically reach. Sniffing and ARP-based on-path attacks threaten confidentiality; SYN floods and amplification threaten availability; worms threaten integrity and control by achieving code execution and replicating autonomously.

Two cross-cutting lessons carry into the rest of the unit. First, the layer of an attack determines both its reach and its defense, Layer 2 attacks are local, Layer 3/4 attacks are global. Second, segmentation shrinks the blast radius of nearly every attack in this topic, which is exactly why it earns its own topic (3.3).

Topic 3.2 takes these same threat categories, sniffing, on-path interception, and rogue infrastructure, and applies them to the wireless medium, where the physical containment we rely on in wired networks simply does not exist.

cover.summary: TCP/IP was built in the 1970s for a small, cooperative research network, and it still assumes trust where a protocol could instead demand proof. This topic examines the attacks that exploit that gap — eavesdropping on a shared medium, forging address bindings, poisoning name resolution, and exhausting the connections a server can hold — and how to reason about the risk each one creates.

big_idea.text: An unencrypted packet crossing a network is a postcard, not a sealed letter. Anyone who handles it in transit can read every word on it without ever needing to open anything.
big_idea.closing: Hold onto this picture — we'll come back to it as the mechanics get more technical.
